title: Anagrams without comparing words
hook: Finding anagrams sounds like checking every pair. What if each word named its own bin?

knows: a hash table groups items by a key (hash-bucket-pileup)
an anagram uses the same letters in a different order
doesNotKnow: that a word's letters in alphabetical order (or its letter counts) is a key shared by all its anagrams

misconception: To find anagrams you must compare each word against every other word.
objective: The learner can explain that sorting each word's letters gives a key that is equal exactly for anagrams, so the ten words listen, silent, enlist, tinsel, google, gogole, cat, act, tac, dog fall into 4 bins (eilnst, eggloo, act, dgo) in one pass, with no word compared to another.

claims.text: With sorted letters as the key, the ten words fall into 4 bins: eilnst (listen, silent, enlist, tinsel), eggloo (google, gogole), act (cat, act, tac) and dgo (dog).
claims.source: Demo.tsx keyOf() / binsFor(), the same code the stage uses; builder re-ran the grouping in a separate node script (scratchpad algo2b0/check.mjs), 2026-10-14. Matches brief cs.algorithms #57. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node: grouping by sorted letters gives eilnst(4) eggloo(2) act(3) dgo(1), same as Demo binsFor.

claims.text: Two words are anagrams exactly when their sorted letters match.
claims.source: Anagrams are rearrangements of the same multiset of letters; sorting maps every arrangement of a multiset to the same string, and two different multisets sort to different strings. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Derivation; independent node check by letter counts finds the same 10 anagram pairs as key equality.

claims.text: Checking every pair of the ten words would take 45 comparisons.
claims.source: 10 choose 2 = 10 x 9 / 2 = 45 (computed in node, scratchpad algo2b0/check2.mjs). · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node: 10 x 9 / 2 = 45 pairs.

claims.text: Grouping by this key needs no word-to-word checks: each word is handled once and sent to the bin its key names; with a hash table, one pass is enough.
claims.source: Hash-table insert and search take O(1) expected time under simple uniform hashing (CLRS 4e ch. 11), so one pass costs expected time linear in the total letters plus the sorting of each word. The stage readout 'Word-to-word checks 0' counts direct comparisons between two words, which the method never makes. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Derivation: each word is keyed and placed once. Note: a hash-table lookup (and Demo's bins.find) compares the new key with stored bin keys; that is key-to-bin, not word-to-word, so the stage's 'Word-to-word checks 0' holds under the claim's own definition. CLRS ch. 11 O(1) expected time from memory, not opened.

recall.question: You must group 10,000 words into anagram families. What key lets you do it in one pass?
options: Each word's first and last letter
recall.why: Anagrams have exactly the same letters, so sorting them gives the same string, and different letters give different strings. Use it as a hash key and each word goes straight to its family.
